title: Clinical support: Practitioner gains may not help patients
desc: Distinguishes clinician performance, patient outcomes, adoption and workflow integration, without establishing broader LLM workforce claims.

kps.k: Clinical decision support offers qualified benefits: better practitioner performance does not necessarily mean better patient outcomes.
kps.d: The cluster concerns how decision support affects clinical practice, rather than establishing AI-driven professional replacement. Negligence and AI's Human Users cites a 2011 synthesis reporting that clinical decision support generally did not improve patient outcomes, although preventive-care reminders and drug-prescription systems could improve provider performance. This distinction makes the choice of outcome central to assessing benefits.

qs.q: INFORMATICS ASS’N 327, 331-32 (2011) (finding that CDS generally did not result in “benefits on patient outcomes” but “can positively impact healthcare providers’ performance with preventative care reminder systems and drug prescription systems”); Kensaku Kawamoto, Caitlin A.
qs.a: Negligence and AI's Human Users · Academia · 2020

kps.k: Adoption and workflow integration shape whether decision support can deliver benefits.
kps.d: Negligence and AI's Human Users cites professional indifference and organisational inertia as barriers to implementation. It also reports a 2005 review associating automatic support within clinician workflows with improved patient outcomes. These findings suggest that implementation deserves attention alongside technical capabilities, but the reported association does not guarantee benefits or establish that workflow integration alone causes them.

kps.k: Specific interventions show different results, not a direct disagreement about decision support as a whole.
kps.d: A study title cited in Large Language Model Influence on Diagnostic Reasoning: A Randomized Clinical Trial reports that early diagnostic suggestions improved GP accuracy in a randomised trial using computer-simulated patients. A title cited in The Effect of AI on the Radiologist Workforce: A Task-Based Analysis reports that an order-entry educational intervention failed to reduce STAT inpatient radiology orders. These findings concern different interventions, settings and outcomes; neither supplies an effect size here, and the simulated-patient result does not establish a benefit in routine clinical care.

kps.k: The supplied material does not establish the parent articles' conclusions about LLM effectiveness, negligence or workforce change.
kps.d: The radiologist-workforce and LLM diagnostic-reasoning excerpts consist of references; the negligence excerpt reports findings from cited literature rather than an independent argument. References identify research on imaging appropriateness, procedure volumes, AI-assisted indication selection, diagnostic-support timing and reflective reasoning, but mostly disclose no results. The practical implication is to distinguish adoption, clinician performance, patient outcomes and service demand when evaluating decision support, without treating these fragments as evidence of employment effects, legal duties or the LLM trial's own findings.

vlens.an: The selected academia and research sources support the cluster’s principal proposition that clinical decision support can improve practitioner performance without necessarily improving patient outcomes, and that adoption and workflow integration condition whether benefits are realised. The strongest substantive evidence distinguishes provider-performance gains from generally absent patient-outcome benefits and identifies integration into clinician workflow as an associated feature. Material internal variation lies in the type and strength of evidence: one source reports these literature findings directly, whereas the other two supplied excerpts are bibliography fragments rather than the parent articles’ own arguments. Those references show intervention-specific variation—early diagnostic suggestions improved GP accuracy in a simulated-patient trial, while an order-entry educational intervention did not reduce STAT radiology orders—but neither establishes routine-care patient benefit, LLM effectiveness, or workforce effects. This assessment applies only to the curated sources supplied and does not indicate the prevalence of this view across academia and research.

elens.an: The 2015–2022 source evidence supports the cluster’s principal proposition that clinical decision support can improve practitioner performance without necessarily improving patient outcomes, and that realised benefits depend materially on adoption and workflow integration. The source reports a distinction between provider-performance gains and generally absent patient-outcome benefits, identifies professional and organisational resistance as an implementation barrier, and associates automatic support embedded in clinician workflow with better outcomes. These are qualified findings rather than claims that decision support is uniformly ineffective or beneficial: effects vary by intervention and outcome, and workflow integration is presented as associated with—not sufficient to guarantee—patient benefit. The evidence does not establish broader claims about LLM effectiveness, professional replacement, negligence or workforce change. Because the period contains one supplied source record, this assessment characterises that source only and does not indicate prevalence across the wider literature.

elens.an: The 2023–2024 source evidence supports the cluster’s principal proposition, but only narrowly. Its strongest cited claim is that early diagnostic suggestions improved GP accuracy in a randomized trial using computer-simulated patients. That is evidence of practitioner-performance improvement in a controlled setting, not evidence of better patient outcomes, routine-care effectiveness, adoption, workflow integration, or workforce change. The remaining references reinforce the cluster’s emphasis on implementation and context by identifying questions about when diagnostic support should enter the diagnostic process and by covering reflective reasoning, bias, and cognitive tools. Material internal variation lies in the types of inquiry represented—one title reports a positive accuracy result, while others merely identify research questions or topics and disclose no findings. Because the supplied excerpts are reference-list material rather than the parent LLM trial’s results or argument, they cannot establish broader claims about LLM effectiveness or clinical impact. This assessment concerns the supplied curated source, not the prevalence of this view among clinical researchers.

elens.an: The 2025 source supports the cluster’s principal proposition chiefly by reinforcing its caution and outcome-specific framing. Its bibliography separates practitioner performance, patient outcomes, imaging appropriateness and procedure volumes rather than treating clinical decision support as producing one uniform benefit. It also identifies a specific intervention that was ineffective, consistent with the proposition that results vary by intervention, setting and outcome. Material variation within the source lies between that explicit negative result and the other cited studies, whose titles identify relevant outcomes but generally do not reveal findings. Because the supplied evidence consists only of bibliography fragments, it cannot establish broad patient benefits, successful adoption at scale, causation from workflow integration, or radiologist workforce effects. This assessment concerns this curated source alone and does not indicate the prevalence of the view among 2025 publications.
